# Should VVT Solenoids be replaced in pairs?

The advice to replace Variable Valve Timing (VVT) solenoids in pairs is a common refrain in automotive repair forums and service manuals. When sourcing parts for a 2011 Skoda Superb 1.8 TSI, you might encounter a specific note from manufacturers like Dorman stating that while there are typically two VVT solenoids per vehicleâone for the left bank and one for the rightâthe failure of one usually indicates the other is not far behind. Manufacturers explicitly recommend replacing them simultaneously. The core question isn't just about following instructions, but understanding the mechanical and electrical realities that make this recommendation sound logical versus a potential marketing tactic to increase parts sales.

To evaluate whether this is good engineering advice or mere upselling, we have to look at how these components function within the engine management system. VVT solenoids are electrically controlled valves that regulate oil pressure to advance or retard the timing of the camshafts. They do not generate their own power; they rely on a steady supply of clean, pressurized engine oil to actuate. This dependency on the lubrication system is the critical factor in shared failure modes.

If a VVT solenoid fails due to internal wear or electrical shorting, it often does so because the oil environment has degraded. Contaminants like sludge, varnish, or metal shavings from other failing engine components can clog the tiny pintle valves inside the solenoid. If you replace only one unit on a 2011 Skoda Superb with an old, dirty oil system, the new solenoid is immediately exposed to the same hostile conditions that killed its predecessor. It is highly probable that the second solenoid has been suffering from similar low-level contamination or minor electrical drift without showing catastrophic symptoms yet. Once one fails completely, the operating environment for the entire system has likely shifted negatively.

From a diagnostic standpoint, treating these components as independent units with vastly different failure rates can lead to premature rework. If you install a new solenoid on the intake bank but leave the old exhaust bank in place, and the vehicle returns to the shop or you experience driveability issues months later, the second replacement is now guaranteed to be necessary because the first one was likely installed into a compromised system.

Consider this scenario: You swap out the failing driver-side solenoid but ignore the passenger side. The car runs fine for six months. Then, under high-load conditions where the ECU demands precise cam timing adjustments, the passenger-side solenoid sticks. Now you are paying to replace parts twice within a reasonable timeframe, plus labor costs for each removal and installation.

There is also the aspect of oil condition. When a VVT solenoid fails, it can sometimes release debris back into the gallery or allow unregulated oil flow that disturbs pressure sensors. While not always the case, cleaning the system or changing the oil when performing this repair is often considered best practice. If you are already disassembling the intake manifold to access one solenoid, the added time to drain the oil, flush the system, and install a fresh filter makes replacing the second unit a logical extension of that labor window.

The decision ultimately rests on risk assessment. Is it cheaper to replace just one part now and accept the statistical probability of a near-future failure on the other side? Or is it more economical to front the cost of two parts and a slightly longer labor session to secure the repair for a longer duration? For a vehicle with high mileage, where access costs are high, the "replace in pairs" approach minimizes the total cost of ownership over the next few years. It treats the VVT solenoids as a system component rather than isolated switches, acknowledging that they share the same life-cycle constraints dictated by oil cleanliness and electrical load cycling.
